what_its_for: This combination medicine is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. Glipizide helps your pancreas release more insulin, and metformin helps your body use insulin better and reduces the amount of sugar your liver makes. Together, they work as a team to keep your blood sugar in a healthy range.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with meals, usually twice a day with your morning and evening meals. Taking it with food helps reduce stomach upset and lowers your risk of low blood sugar. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablet unless your doctor tells you it is okay. Take it at the same times each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how well your blood sugar is controlled. A common starting dose is one tablet of glipizide 2.5 mg and metformin 250 mg or 500 mg twice daily with meals. The dose is adjusted every 2 weeks as needed. Do not change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember with your next meal. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could cause dangerously low blood sugar.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can cause your blood sugar to drop too low and may increase the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. Avoid skipping meals, as this can cause low blood sugar. Be careful with activities that require alertness, like driving, if you feel dizzy or shaky. Tell your doctor before having any surgery, X-ray with contrast dye, or other procedures, because you may need to temporarily stop this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: signs of low blood sugar such as shaking, sweating, dizziness, fast heartbeat, confusion, or blurred vision; signs of lactic acidosis such as muscle pain, weakness, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, feeling cold, or unusual tiredness; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; yellowing of the skin or eyes; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Metformin usually starts working within a few days, but it may take 2 to 3 months to see the full benefit on your blood sugar levels. Glipizide can start lowering blood sugar within 1 to 2 hours of your first dose. Your doctor will check your blood sugar and a lab test called HbA1c every 3 months to see how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to this medicine and have a higher risk of low blood sugar and lactic acidosis, so lower doses may be used. This medicine is not recommended for use during pregnancy; talk to your doctor about safer options if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk, so tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding. This medicine is not approved for use in children. People with kidney problems may not be able to take metformin safely, so your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment.
